prerequisites: Prior mathematical knowledge acquired with the "Fundamentals of Mathematics" course of the first semester.

learning_outcomes.text: Knowledge of the scientific method, classical physics, kinematics, dynamics, fluids, thermodynamics, electromagnetism, electromagnetic waves.

Ability to set up and solve a classical physics problem, describe the classical physical world with appropriate physical quantities and their relationships, and correctly and quantitatively predict the evolution of a physical process.

Ability to identify, in written form, for a given problem, the physical quantities involved, their relationships, and exact or approximate numerical ratios, through in-class examples related to the theoretical part, written exercises during the course, tutor help with exercises, and a final written exam.

Ability to describe the physical framework and developments of a proposed situation through specific questions on predictions concerning the explained physical theory. Ability to describe in words and formulas the main topics of the subject and their implications during a final oral examination.

Autonomously recognize the essential terms of a classical physical phenomenon, identify the physical quantities involved, their relationships, and the system's evolution over time. Hypothesize modifications to achieve a desired different outcome, set up and quantitatively solve physical problems encountered or intended. Constructively relate to measurement apparatus necessary for the quantitative study of the phenomenon.

Recognize the essential terms of a classical physical phenomenon, of mechanics, thermodynamics, and electromagnetism, meaning the physical quantities involved, their relationships, and the system's evolution over time.
Distinguish between experimentally obtained results and theoretical ones derived from mathematical models and then compared with experiment.

Solve problems in mechanics, thermodynamics, and electromagnetism, recognizing the physical quantities involved, their relationships, and exact or approximate numerical ratios, knowing how to correctly and quantitatively predict the evolution of a physical process.

Describe in words and with formulas the main topics of the subject and their implications, knowing how to connect different similar topics starting from a single specific case, demonstrating the ability to reason about the various related aspects.

syllabus_topics: Kinematics of a point: Introduction to mechanics. Properties of vectors. Time law and trajectory of a material point. Varied motion in the plane and in space. Rectilinear motion, uniform and accelerated. Vertical motion in a gravitational field. Simple harmonic motion. Circular motion. Parabolic motion of bodies in a gravitational field.

Dynamics of a point: Principle of inertia and Newton's laws. Momentum and impulse. Resultant of forces, equilibrium, constraint reactions and centripetal forces. Weight force, elastic force, static and viscous friction force. Applications on an inclined plane. Tension of wires and simple pendulum. Work, kinetic energy. Conservative and non-conservative forces and potential energy. Angular momentum and central forces.
Relative motion: Reference frames, relative velocities and accelerations. Inertial reference frames and Galilean relativity. Uniform rectilinear dragging motion.

Systems of material points: Internal and external forces in a system of material points. Center of Mass (CM) and theorem of CM motion. Conservation of momentum. Theorem and conservation of angular momentum. CM reference frame. Konig's theorems and kinetic energy theorem. Collisions between material points (elastic, inelastic, completely inelastic collision).

Rigid body dynamics: Definition of a rigid body. Motion of a rigid body. Continuous body, density and CM position. Rigid rotations around a fixed axis. Moment of inertia. Huygens-Steiner theorem. Pure rolling motion. Angular impulse, impulse moment. Conservation laws in rigid body motion. Collisions between rigid bodies and material points.
Gravitation: Gravitational force. Inertial mass and gravitational mass. Gravitational field. Gravitational potential energy.

Thermodynamics: Thermodynamic state and equilibrium. Temperature. First Law of Thermodynamics. Internal Energy. Thermodynamic transformations, Work and Heat. Calorimetry. Isothermal processes. Phase changes. Ideal gases. Gas transformations and work. Heat and specific heats. Internal energy of an ideal gas. Ideal gas transformations and cyclic transformations: Carnot cycle and refrigeration cycles. Real gases and phase changes. Kinetic theory of ideal gases: pressure calculation and energy equipartition. Second Law of Thermodynamics. Carnot and Clausius theorems. Entropy.

Electrostatics in vacuum: Experimental aspects of interactions between electric charges: Coulomb's law. Operational definition and properties of the electrostatic field. Electrostatic field generated by systems of charges with fixed and known spatial distribution. Flux of a vector: Gauss's theorem or divergence theorem. Maxwell's first equation. Electrostatic potential. Electric dipole: potential and field. Mechanical actions on electric dipoles in an external electric field. Curl of a vector field and conservativeness of the electrostatic field. Potential energy of a set of charges. Energy of the electrostatic field.

The electrostatic field in the presence of conductors in equilibrium: Electric field inside and on the surface of a conductor in equilibrium. Distribution of charges on the surface of conductors. The general problem of electrostatics in vacuum. System of two conductors: the electric capacitor. Capacitance of a capacitor, in plane, spherical and cylindrical cases. Capacitance of a thin capacitor. Series and parallel capacitors. Energy of the electrostatic field in the presence of conductors in equilibrium: energy stored in a capacitor.

Stationary electric currents: Conductors, charges, fields and electromotive force. Current density and intensity. Continuity equation. Ohm's law: conductivity, resistivity, resistance. Electrical resistance of ohmic conducting structures; series and parallel resistances. Electric field in conductors in stationary conditions. Electromotive force and electric generators. Electrical power dissipated in a circuit and Joule's law. Conservation of electric charge. Circuits with quasi-stationary current. Charging and discharging a capacitor with energy considerations (fRC and RC circuits).

Magnetostatics in vacuum: Lorentz force and magnetic induction vector: operational definition. Motion of a charge in an electric and magnetic field. Flux of the magnetic induction vector. Magnetic force on a current-carrying wire: Laplace's second formula. Mechanical actions on circuits with stationary current in an external magnetic field. Sources of the magnetic field and experimental aspects. Laplace's first law. Magnetic fields created by particular current distributions; infinite straight wire (Biot-Savart law), circular loop (on axis), solenoid. Definition of Ampere; magnetic dipole moment of a loop; circulation of a vector field and Ampere's theorem; Gauss's law for the magnetic field; the equations of magnetostatics in integral and differential form. Interactions between circuits with stationary current.

Time-varying electric and magnetic fields: Electromagnetic induction: Faraday-Neumann-Lenz law. Induced electromotive force. Variation of concatenated flux due to variation of the supply current of the source circuits. Foucault currents. Curl of the electric field: local form of Faraday-Neumann law and expression of Maxwell's third equation in the non-stationary case. Mutual and self-induction. The transformer principle. fRL and RL circuits.

Maxwell's equations and electromagnetic waves: Displacement current; Maxwell's equations in vacuum in integral and differential form; wave equation in electromagnetism; propagation speed of electromagnetic waves; plane waves in vacuum. Energy conservation and Poynting vector. Sources of the EM field. Spectrum of EM waves.

assessment_methods.method: Written exam consisting of solving mechanics, thermodynamics, and electromagnetism problems
Oral exam (if written exam is passed)

assessment_rules: Students must pass a written exam consisting of solving problems in mechanics, thermodynamics, and electromagnetism. If the written exam is sufficient, the student's evaluation will be completed with an oral exam.
